candidateA.name: numeric-generation-authority
candidateA.security: weak against same-label/different-content and rollback confusion
candidateA.complexity: low protocol change, high hidden invalidation complexity
candidateA.memoryLatency: fast lookup but stale evaluator/index risk
candidateA.rollbackCrashRecovery: numeric ordering can accept the wrong content after crash or label reuse
candidateA.leanRustBenchmark: requires numeric authority and cannot prove content equality without extra bindings

candidateB.name: fully-content-addressed-product-identity
candidateB.security: strong exact identity and fail-closed cross-content rejection
candidateB.complexity: higher digest construction and propagation cost
candidateB.memoryLatency: larger keys and validation cost, bounded by server-owned immutable indexes
candidateB.rollbackCrashRecovery: safe only when commit/CAS and durable snapshot are authoritative
candidateB.leanRustBenchmark: best content-binding proof surface, but epoch/fencing concerns remain

candidateC.name: content-digest-product-identity-with-monotonic-epoch-fence
candidateC.security: content correctness is digest-bound; epoch cannot override digest mismatch
candidateC.migration: supports V1 seam while removing epoch from public identity later
candidateC.complexity: moderate: separate identity, commit, fence, and telemetry types
candidateC.memoryLatency: content-keyed resident reuse; epoch is scalar metadata, not cache key
candidateC.rollbackCrashRecovery: single durable content commit plus CAS expected digest; epoch only orders actor work
candidateC.leanRustBenchmark: maps cleanly to content identity, single commit, cancellation, and no-cross-content proofs

designReview.reason: Candidate C appears to remove the observed identity conflations while preserving a reversible V1 migration seam; candidateA appears unable to prevent stale content, and candidateB alone does not define actor fencing or crash ordering.
